title: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Conversational Home Energy Management Systems
summary: The growing complexity in home energy management (HEM) demands advanced systems that guide occupants toward informed energy decisions reflecting their background, preferences, and context. Large language model (LLM)-integrated HEM systems (HEMS) have demonstrated promise, but previous studies relied on single-turn or single-task evaluations with response accuracy as the primary metric. Whether such systems deliver effective interactions across the extended multi-turn dialogues typical of real-world use remains an open question. This study introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework of LLM-integrated HEMS derived from the Goal-Question-Metric methodology, organized across five categories: task performance, factual accuracy, interaction quality, control capability, and system efficiency. A total of 23 metrics across multi-turn conversations are proposed and an LLM-as-judge pipeline is employed to enable scalable automated scoring. Its reliability is validated against three trained human coders: after iterative rubric calibration, twelve of the fifteen LLM-scored metrics reached strong agreement (ICC >= 0.73), three of them perfect, while the remaining three exhibited near-zero variance in human scores and are instead reported via mean absolute error (0.04-0.28). To demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, 970 dialogues -- 16 scenarios and five personas -- were generated and evaluated across four conversational HEMS configurations spanning a sophistication gradient, from a vanilla LLM with raw energy data to a multi-agent HEMS. The framework distinguished the four configurations across multiple evaluation dimensions, revealing their respective strengths and weaknesses. This study contributes to conversational HEMS by providing a reproducible, multi-dimensional evaluation methodology that comprehensively assesses sustained, context-aware system performance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents and validates a multidimensional framework for evaluating LLM-integrated home energy management systems (HEMS) in sustained, multi-turn conversations. It defines 23 metrics in five categories and uses a calibrated LLM-as-judge pipeline validated against human coders. Evaluation of 970 dialogues across 16 scenarios, five personas, and four HEMS configurations shows that the framework can differentiate system capabilities and limitations.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-integrated HEMS largely focus on single-turn or single-task settings and prioritize response accuracy. These approaches do not adequately measure the sustained, context-aware interactions, personalized decision support, control actions, and efficiency required in realistic home energy management. The paper therefore seeks a reproducible and comprehensive evaluation methodology for multi-turn HEMS interactions.
AI.method: The authors develop a Goal-Question-Metric-based evaluation framework covering five dimensions: task performance, factual accuracy, interaction quality, control capability, and system efficiency. The framework contains 23 metrics evaluated over multi-turn dialogues. An LLM-as-judge pipeline provides scalable automated scoring, with its reliability assessed against three trained human coders through iterative rubric calibration. For demonstration, the authors generate and evaluate 970 dialogues spanning 16 scenarios and five personas across four HEMS configurations arranged along a sophistication gradient, from a vanilla LLM using raw energy data to a multi-agent HEMS.
AI.result: After rubric calibration, 12 of 15 LLM-scored metrics achieved strong agreement with human judgments (ICC >= 0.73), including three with perfect agreement. The remaining three metrics had near-zero variance in human ratings and were assessed using mean absolute error, ranging from 0.04 to 0.28. The framework successfully differentiated the four HEMS configurations across multiple dimensions and exposed their distinct strengths and weaknesses.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes a reproducible, multidimensional approach for assessing LLM-integrated HEMS under realistic multi-turn interaction conditions. Its validated automated evaluation pipeline supports scalable comparison of system performance beyond response accuracy, although the reported validation is based on three human coders and the demonstration relies on generated dialogues and selected configurations.

title: Critsly and StudioCrit: An Artefact-Aware AI Critique Workspace and Simulation-Based Readiness Study for Design Education
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Technical report adapted from an SMT 99.580 research project submitted on 23 July 2026. Documents StudioCrit engineering and simulation evidence; related Critsly demo: arXiv:2607.09673. No human-participant learning outcomes are reported
summary: Critique in design education depends on interpreting work in progress, articulating intentions and translating feedback into revisions. This technical report presents Critsly, an artefact-aware AI critique workspace, and StudioCrit, its architecture-studio research mode. Critsly combines a visual board, design-intention fields, guided reflection, perspective-based critique and action planning. StudioCrit adds studio/class organisation, role-based access, cognitive and architectural classification, educator analytics and exportable evidence. The report consolidates implementation and simulation evidence recorded in a research project submitted in July 2026. Three simulated studio scenarios yielded 109 classified evidence rows, including 85 assigned to higher-order Bloom categories. A separate rehearsal using 50 disposable learner accounts yielded 56 evidence rows, including 46 assigned to higher-order categories. A subsequent hardening rehearsal recorded 50 completed sessions, 50 successful board pulls and 50 denials of student access to analytics. These are software and synthetic-trace observations, not measurements of learning gains or human cognitive performance. Automated classifications remain provisional, and the source report does not establish classifier accuracy or inter-rater reliability. The contribution is an implemented critique-to-evidence workflow and a bounded account of its readiness for further controlled evaluation.

AI.tldr: Critsly and its StudioCrit mode are implemented AI-supported design-critique workspaces that structure intentions, feedback, reflection, and revision planning while generating classified evidence for educators. The report presents software and synthetic-trace results—not evidence of learning gains—and identifies classification validity as unresolved.
AI.motivation: Design critique requires learners to interpret unfinished work, express design intentions, use feedback, and convert critique into concrete revisions. Existing critique workflows may not systematically connect these activities to artefacts, educational roles, and auditable evidence. The paper is motivated by the need for an integrated workspace that supports critique while making the resulting process traceable for research and teaching.
AI.method: The authors implemented Critsly, an artefact-aware AI critique workspace, and StudioCrit, an architecture-studio research mode. The system combines a visual board, intention fields, guided reflection, perspective-based critique, action planning, studio/class organisation, role-based access, cognitive and architectural classification, educator analytics, and exportable evidence. Evaluation consisted of three simulated studio scenarios producing 109 classified evidence rows, a rehearsal with 50 disposable learner accounts producing 56 rows, and a hardening rehearsal involving 50 completed sessions, 50 successful board retrievals, and 50 denials of student access to analytics. Automated classifications were treated as provisional, with no reported classifier-accuracy or inter-rater-reliability assessment.
AI.result: The implementation generated structured critique evidence: 109 rows in the simulated studio scenarios, including 85 classified in higher-order Bloom categories; 56 rows in the disposable-account rehearsal, including 46 higher-order rows; and successful completion, board retrieval, and access-control outcomes in all 50 hardening sessions. These findings demonstrate workflow operation and basic system-readiness properties. They do not demonstrate learning improvement, cognitive performance, or valid classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The report contributes an implemented critique-to-evidence workflow and a bounded readiness assessment for future controlled research. Its main value is system integration and traceability rather than educational efficacy. Further studies should use real learners and educators, predefined evaluation criteria, independent or multiple coders, classifier-validation and reliability analyses, and controlled designs measuring learning and revision outcomes.

title: When the AI Leaves the Tailorshop: Measuring What an LLM Advisor Leaves Behind in Complex Problem Solving
summary: Complex problem solving depends on acting effectively and understanding how a system works. AI advice may support these outcomes unequally. Two preregistered experiments compared participants managing a simulated clothing factory with and without an LLM advisor. Across studies, AI-supported participants reported greater confidence and understanding with less effort. In the first study (N=200), assistance increased company value but produced no detectable prediction-accuracy difference. After withdrawal, previously supported participants outperformed controls when decisions were scored against repeating previous choices, but not default settings. Within the AI-supported group, more frequent recommendation alterations predicted better unaided performance. In the second study (N=198), AI-supported participants went bankrupt less often and showed a small knowledge advantage in the registered analysis, largely associated with remaining solvent. More frequent recommendation alterations predicted higher knowledge within the AI-supported group. Applied HAI evaluation should assess users' understanding and independent capability alongside the performance achieved with AI support.

AI.tldr: Two preregistered experiments tested whether LLM advice improves not only immediate performance in a simulated clothing factory, but also users’ understanding and independent decision-making after AI support is removed. AI assistance improved confidence, perceived understanding, and often operational outcomes, while evidence for transfer to unaided performance was mixed and depended on the evaluation criterion. Users who more actively modified recommendations tended to perform better independently and demonstrate greater knowledge.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a central question in human-AI interaction: whether AI advice genuinely develops users’ understanding and independent capability, or merely improves task performance while support is available. This distinction is important for evaluating complex problem solving and for designing applied HAI assessments that do not equate AI-assisted success with human learning.
AI.method: The researchers conducted two preregistered experiments using a simulated clothing-factory management task. Participants were assigned to manage the system with or without an LLM advisor. Outcomes included company value, bankruptcy or solvency, prediction accuracy, knowledge, confidence, perceived understanding, effort, and performance after AI withdrawal. The analyses also examined whether the frequency with which participants altered AI recommendations predicted later unaided performance or knowledge.
AI.result: Across both studies, AI-supported participants reported higher confidence and understanding while exerting less effort. In Study 1 (N=200), AI assistance increased company value but did not produce a detectable improvement in prediction accuracy. After the advisor was removed, AI-supported participants outperformed controls when evaluated against repeated prior choices, but not when evaluated against default settings. Within the supported group, more frequent recommendation changes predicted better unaided performance. In Study 2 (N=198), AI-supported participants went bankrupt less often and showed a small registered knowledge advantage, largely associated with remaining solvent. More frequent recommendation changes again predicted greater knowledge.
AI.conclusion: LLM advice can improve immediate task outcomes and may provide some transfer to independent performance and knowledge, but these benefits are inconsistent and sensitive to how independent capability is measured. Active engagement with, rather than passive acceptance of, recommendations appears related to better learning. HAI evaluations should therefore measure users’ understanding, confidence, effort, and unaided capability in addition to performance achieved with AI assistance.

title: Three Pathways of Student-AI Interaction: Constraint-First Design for Higher-Order Thinking
summary: How students interact with artificial intelligence (AI) systems in educational settings may determine whether that interaction supports or displaces critical thinking. This paper introduces two contributions. The first is the Three Paths of Student-AI Interaction, a typological framework identifying three qualitatively distinct modes of student-AI engagement: Passive Review, Direct Question, and Strategic Dialogue. The second is the Next Level Teaching Blueprint (NLTB), a three-stage instructional design system intended to make Strategic Dialogue more likely. Qualitative content analysis of 50 randomly sampled student-AI interaction messages from an undergraduate research methods course was used to examine the typology. Two human coders achieved 68% path-level agreement ($κ$ = .48), with 80% agreement on Strategic Dialogue identification specifically. GPT-5, used as a third coder, produced a similar overall distribution and introduced a coding category absent from the human scheme. Path 1 (Passive Review) accounted for 46% of exchanges in the primary researcher's classifications, Path 2 (Direct Question) for 18%, and Path 3 (Strategic Dialogue) for 36%. A second, descriptively examined dataset contained predominantly Strategic Dialogue content, offering a preliminary indication that instructional framing may influence which path students take. Together, the Three Paths framework and the NLTB contribute a language for describing student-AI interaction and a design approach for supporting higher-order engagement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a three-part framework for classifying student–AI interaction and an instructional design system intended to promote the most cognitively demanding interaction mode. Using qualitative coding of 50 messages, it finds that passive review was most common, while strategic dialogue accounted for over one-third of exchanges. The findings are preliminary because the sample is small, agreement between human coders was moderate, and the second dataset was only descriptively examined.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by concern that student use of AI in education may either support or displace critical thinking. Existing discussions often treat AI interaction as a single phenomenon, so the authors seek a vocabulary for distinguishing different levels of student engagement and a teaching approach that may encourage more reflective, higher-order use.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Three Paths of Student-AI Interaction: Passive Review, Direct Question, and Strategic Dialogue. They also propose the three-stage Next Level Teaching Blueprint (NLTB), designed to increase the likelihood of Strategic Dialogue. To examine the typology, they conduct qualitative content analysis on 50 randomly sampled messages from an undergraduate research methods course. Two human coders independently classified the messages, and GPT-5 served as an additional coder. Agreement was assessed using percentage agreement and Cohen’s kappa. A second dataset was examined descriptively rather than through formal inferential analysis.
AI.result: In the primary researcher’s classification, Passive Review represented 46% of exchanges, Direct Question 18%, and Strategic Dialogue 36%. The two human coders achieved 68% path-level agreement, corresponding to κ = .48, which indicates moderate agreement; agreement for identifying Strategic Dialogue specifically was 80%. GPT-5 generated a broadly similar distribution and also proposed a category not present in the human coding scheme. The second dataset consisted predominantly of Strategic Dialogue, providing preliminary descriptive evidence that instructional framing may shape students’ interaction patterns.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a practical language for differentiating student–AI engagement and an instructional design proposal for promoting strategic, higher-order dialogue. However, the evidence should be interpreted as exploratory: the sample is limited, coder agreement is not strong, GPT-5’s role raises methodological questions, and the second dataset does not support causal claims about the NLTB. Further research should test the framework with larger and more diverse samples, clearer coding criteria, and controlled comparisons of instructional conditions.

title: Faithful Chart Generation for Multimodal Deep Research: Frame-Evidence Co-Adaptation
summary: Analytical charts in multimodal deep research encode quantitative claims, requiring every visualized value to be faithfully grounded in supporting evidence. Unlike retrieved images that mainly provide contextual information, charts require numerical fidelity: visualized values should not only match retrieved evidence quantitatively but also preserve its original meaning and scope. However, achieving such fidelity remains challenging because current systems usually construct visualization plans before knowing what quantitative evidence can actually be retrieved from the web. As a result, predefined plans may require entities, temporal ranges, or comparison dimensions that the retrieved evidence only partially supports. Existing approaches mainly address this issue through post-hoc verification after chart plans are fixed, enabling unsupported values to be identified but leaving the underlying visual frames unchanged. To address this challenge, we propose Frame-Evidence Co-Adaptation (FECA), an evidence-adaptive visual planning framework for multimodal deep research. Inspired by the bidirectional sensemaking process in Data-Frame Theory, FECA models chart generation as an iterative interaction between visual frames and retrieved evidence. Each visual frame is adaptive: the frame guides evidence acquisition, while retrieved evidence determines whether the frame should be accepted, revised, or dropped before rendering. By coupling visualization planning with evidence availability, FECA shifts chart generation from fixed-plan verification to adaptive evidence-grounded visual reasoning. Experiments on 100 real-world research topics show that FECA substantially improves numerical fidelity while preserving report quality and chart utility.

AI.tldr: FECA is an evidence-adaptive chart-generation framework that iteratively co-adapts visualization frames and retrieved evidence to improve the numerical fidelity and utility of analytical charts in multimodal deep research.
AI.motivation: Analytical charts must faithfully represent quantitative evidence, including its values, meaning, and scope. Existing systems typically fix visualization plans before retrieval and only perform post-hoc verification, so unsupported entities, time ranges, or comparisons can be detected but the visual frame itself remains unchanged. The paper addresses this mismatch between predefined chart plans and the evidence actually available on the web.
AI.method: Frame-Evidence Co-Adaptation (FECA) models chart generation as an iterative interaction between visual frames and retrieved evidence, drawing on Data-Frame Theory. A visual frame guides evidence acquisition, while the retrieved evidence determines whether the frame is accepted, revised, or dropped before rendering. This couples visualization planning with evidence availability rather than treating verification as a post-hoc step.
AI.result: Experiments on 100 real-world research topics show that FECA substantially improves numerical fidelity while preserving report quality and chart utility. The abstract does not provide quantitative performance values, baselines, or statistical significance details.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive co-design between chart frames and retrievable evidence is more effective than fixing chart plans and verifying them afterward. FECA shifts chart generation toward evidence-grounded visual reasoning, enabling charts that are better supported without sacrificing usefulness or overall report quality.

title: Preliminary Evaluation of Transition-Aware Controller Locomotion Adaptations for Supporting Postural Stability in VR
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, accepted in ISMAR 2026 poster track
summary: We present three locomotion adaptation approaches: Motion Acceleration, Turn Acceleration, and Motion Deceleration to improve postural stability during body-state transitions in virtual reality (VR). The system detects standing-to-walking, turning, and walking-to-stopping transitions and applies adaptive locomotion smoothing. Motion Acceleration gradually increases locomotion speed when users begin walking, Turn Acceleration smooths rotation while turning, and Motion Deceleration gradually reduces movement speed before stopping. We evaluated these techniques in a virtual navigation task using objective and subjective balance measures. Preliminary results show reduced center of pressure (COP) velocity and improved balance confidence. These findings suggest that locomotion adaptations can improve balance and navigation experience.

AI.tldr: This paper presents and preliminarily evaluates three adaptive VR locomotion techniques—Motion Acceleration, Turn Acceleration, and Motion Deceleration—to improve postural stability during transitions between standing, walking, turning, and stopping. The techniques reduce center-of-pressure velocity and improve users’ balance confidence during virtual navigation.
AI.motivation: Conventional or abrupt virtual locomotion transitions may induce instability and reduce users’ confidence, particularly when users start walking, turn, or stop. The paper is motivated by the need to make VR navigation smoother and safer by adapting movement speed and rotation to users’ body-state transitions.
AI.method: The system detects three transition types: standing-to-walking, turning, and walking-to-stopping. It applies three corresponding smoothing mechanisms: Motion Acceleration gradually increases locomotion speed at walking onset; Turn Acceleration smooths rotational movement during turns; and Motion Deceleration gradually decreases speed before stopping. The approaches were evaluated in a virtual navigation task using objective postural measures, including center-of-pressure (COP) velocity, and subjective measures of balance confidence.
AI.result: Preliminary findings indicate that the adaptive locomotion techniques reduce COP velocity and improve reported balance confidence. These results suggest better postural control and a more comfortable navigation experience compared with less-adaptive locomotion transitions, although the abstract does not report statistical significance, sample size, or detailed comparative results.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive smoothing of locomotion speed and rotation can improve balance-related outcomes during VR body-state transitions. The findings support transition-aware locomotion design for enhancing VR navigation stability and user experience, while further research is needed to confirm the effects with larger samples and more comprehensive comparisons.

title: Sensing Instability, Adapting the Scene: A Real-Time Movement-Smoothing Design Framework for Stable VR Locomotion
comment: 3 pages, accepted as ISMAR 2026 AXR workshop paper
summary: Users experience different balance challenges while standing, walking, and turning in virtual reality (VR), yet most locomotion techniques apply the same visual behavior regardless of movement state. We present a real-time movement-smoothing design framework in this paper that organizes visual adaptations according to movement-specific balance demands. The framework introduces three design strategies targeting standing, walking, and turning, illustrating how state-aware visual adaptations can support postural stability during locomotion. This paper focuses on the framework design and implementation, while a user study is planned as future work. Our work guides the development of future context-aware VR locomotion systems that better support safe and comfortable navigation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a real-time, movement-state-aware visual-smoothing framework for VR locomotion. It adapts visual behavior differently during standing, walking, and turning to address their distinct balance demands. The framework is implemented and illustrated through three design strategies, but its effectiveness has not yet been empirically evaluated because the user study is planned for future work.
AI.motivation: Existing VR locomotion techniques generally use uniform visual behavior across different movement states. This may overlook the distinct postural and balance challenges associated with standing, walking, and turning, potentially reducing user stability, comfort, and safety. The paper therefore aims to organize visual adaptations around movement-specific balance demands.
AI.method: The authors design and implement a real-time movement-smoothing framework that recognizes or distinguishes standing, walking, and turning states. It provides three corresponding visual-adaptation strategies, each tailored to the balance requirements of one movement state. The work is primarily a design and implementation contribution rather than an empirical evaluation.
AI.result: The paper presents the framework and demonstrates how state-aware visual adaptations can be applied to standing, walking, and turning during VR locomotion. However, no user-study results are reported, so improvements in postural stability, comfort, or safety remain unverified.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a context-aware approach for developing safer and more comfortable VR locomotion systems by adapting visual smoothing to the user’s movement state. Its practical and perceptual benefits require validation in the planned future user study.

title: From Images to Tasks: Characterizing Multimodal LLM Interactions in the Wild
summary: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) increasingly integrate vision and text, yet how people use them in natural settings remains underexplored. We seek to answer the question: when users upload images, what tasks are they trying to accomplish? Analyzing over 40,000 de-identified image-upload conversations from Microsoft Copilot, we characterize real-world multimodal use through a hierarchical framework of ten capabilities, spanning perception, cognition, and generation. First, we characterize the distribution and composition of these capabilities, finding that the majority of image-upload tasks involve multiple capabilities. Second, we find that multimodal use spans a broader and more diverse task space than text-only interactions, with asymmetric coverage and task classes that rely on cross-modal grounding. Third, mapping observed capability demand onto 253 existing benchmarks reveals uneven alignment between benchmark coverage and real-world use: benchmarks concentrate on perception and reasoning toward fixed answers, while common workflows involving text, code, and data generation remain comparatively undertested. We validate our taxonomy and findings on an independent ChatGPT dataset. Our results provide a large-scale empirical characterization of what users seek to accomplish with multimodal LLMs and highlight opportunities for benchmark design grounded in observed user demand.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how people use multimodal LLMs in real-world image-upload conversations. Using more than 40,000 de-identified Microsoft Copilot conversations and an independent ChatGPT dataset, it proposes a ten-capability taxonomy, compares multimodal and text-only task distributions, and evaluates how well existing benchmarks reflect actual user needs.
AI.motivation: Real-world use of multimodal LLMs is not well understood. Existing evaluations often emphasize isolated perception or reasoning tasks, creating uncertainty about whether benchmarks represent the broader, compositional workflows users perform with uploaded images. The paper aims to identify users’ actual goals and expose gaps between observed demand and benchmark coverage.
AI.method: The authors analyze over 40,000 de-identified image-upload conversations from Microsoft Copilot and organize them using a hierarchical framework of ten capabilities covering perception, cognition, and generation. They compare multimodal task diversity with text-only interactions, identify tasks requiring cross-modal grounding, map capability demand to 253 existing benchmarks, and validate the taxonomy and findings using an independent ChatGPT dataset.
AI.result: Most image-upload conversations involve multiple capabilities rather than a single function. Multimodal interactions cover a broader and more diverse task space than text-only interactions, with uneven capability coverage and substantial demand for cross-modal grounding. Existing benchmarks are concentrated on perception and fixed-answer reasoning, while common workflows involving text, code, and data generation receive comparatively little evaluation coverage. The findings are replicated on the independent ChatGPT dataset.
AI.conclusion: Real-world multimodal LLM use is broad, compositional, and substantially different from the narrow task distribution represented by many current benchmarks. Benchmark development should be guided by observed user demand and should more adequately evaluate multimodal workflows involving generation, transformation, and integration of visual, textual, code, and data outputs.

title: LeanSide: A Formally Verified Co-Reasoning System for Natural-language Proofs
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as collaborators on deductive-reasoning tasks, but their outputs can hallucinate or pull users away from intended reasoning. Formal proof assistants provide machine-checked verification, but have a steep learning curve and require more granular reasoning than human written proofs. We explore an interface that combines these strengths, allowing users to write and revise free-form natural-language proofs while a verified backend checks their reasoning and returns feedback at the user's granularity. We study this interface in the context of undergraduate mathematics education by developing LeanSide, a formally verified co-reasoning system, which auto-formalizes student reasoning into Lean and informalizes verifier output into understandable feedback. We conducted user studies through classroom deployment and analyzed which system properties helped students make progress and which caused them to get stuck. We use these findings to derive design implications for using a formally verified backend in human-AI co-reasoning systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LeanSide, a system that lets students write free-form natural-language mathematical proofs while a Lean-based verified backend checks the reasoning and provides feedback in understandable, user-level language. Classroom studies examine how this human-AI co-reasoning interface supports or impedes students’ progress and derive design implications.
AI.motivation: Large language models can produce incorrect reasoning or distract users from their intended proof strategies, while formal proof assistants offer reliable verification but demand specialized syntax and fine-grained formal reasoning. The paper addresses this usability and reliability gap by exploring an interface that preserves natural-language interaction while retaining machine-checked verification, particularly for undergraduate mathematics education.
AI.method: The authors developed LeanSide, a formally verified co-reasoning system. Students write and revise proofs in natural language; the system auto-formalizes their reasoning into Lean, uses Lean to verify it, and translates verifier outputs back into feedback aligned with the student’s level of granularity. The system was evaluated through classroom deployment and qualitative analysis of the system properties that helped students advance or caused them to become stuck.
AI.result: The studies identified both beneficial and problematic properties of the interface, including how automated formalization and feedback affected students’ ability to make progress. The abstract does not report quantitative outcomes, but indicates that the classroom analysis revealed concrete interaction patterns and failure modes relevant to system design.
AI.conclusion: Combining natural-language proof authoring with a formally verified backend is a promising approach to human-AI co-reasoning in mathematics education. However, effective systems must carefully manage the alignment between student-level reasoning, formal verification requirements, and the granularity and interpretability of feedback.

title: Scaling Peer Assessments: An Integrity Report from a Large Engineering Internship
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables; submitted to ICTIEE and under review
summary: Assessing learning in large classrooms presents a significant challenge for individual instructors, who may have limited capacity to evaluate the understanding, participation, and assessment behaviour of every student. Peer assessments have been a way of distributing this responsibility among learners, allowing them to evaluate and provide feedback to one another while reducing dependence on instructor-led assessments. Building on this approach, we implemented a peer validation model within a large, multi-institutional internship programme in which students who demonstrated sufficient understanding were authorised to assess and validate their peers through short oral discussions. The assessment process began with the instructor validating a small group of students, who were then authorised to validate their peers, allowing the process to gradually expand across the cohort and operate at scale. This study examines how participants experienced the model and the extent to which assessment integrity was maintained, using an end-of-programme survey of 238 consenting respondents. Most participants regarded the activity as worthwhile, with 79.8% reporting that they solved problems they could not previously solve. However, 29.0% acknowledged at least one instance of reduced effort, a lowered validation standard, or reciprocal validation, while 88.7% believed that at least a little validation had occurred without proper examination. When asked how the process could be strengthened, participants selected post-validation discussion of solutions approximately twice as often as closer auditing or mentor-led validation. These findings provide descriptive evidence of both the potential and the integrity challenges of using peer validation as a scalable assessment approach in large learning environments.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a scalable peer-validation assessment model in a large, multi-institutional internship programme. Students initially validated by instructors were authorised to assess peers through brief oral discussions. Survey results suggest the model was perceived as useful and supported learning, but its assessment integrity was imperfect, with reported reduced effort, lenient standards, reciprocal validation, and suspected validations without adequate examination.
AI.motivation: Large classes and multi-institutional programmes make it difficult for instructors to assess every student’s understanding, participation, and assessment behaviour directly. The study is motivated by the need for an assessment model that distributes evaluation responsibilities while preserving learning benefits and sufficient assessment integrity.
AI.method: The authors implemented a cascading peer-validation model. Instructors first validated a small group of students; these students then validated peers who demonstrated sufficient understanding, allowing the process to scale across the cohort. The study used an end-of-programme survey of 238 consenting participants to examine their experiences and perceptions of assessment integrity. The analysis was primarily descriptive, reporting participant responses to the value of the activity, problematic validation behaviours, suspected inadequate examinations, and possible improvement measures.
AI.result: Most respondents viewed the activity positively, and 79.8% reported solving problems they had previously been unable to solve. Nevertheless, 29.0% reported at least one integrity concern involving reduced effort, lowered standards, or reciprocal validation. A larger proportion, 88.7%, believed that some validation had occurred without proper examination. Participants favoured post-validation discussions of solutions as an improvement, selecting this option about twice as often as closer auditing or mentor-led validation.
AI.conclusion: Peer validation appears promising for supporting learning and scaling assessment in large cohorts, but the model faces substantial integrity risks. The findings support using structured peer validation with additional safeguards, particularly post-validation solution discussions and mechanisms for monitoring or auditing validation quality. Because the evidence is based on self-reported survey data from consenting respondents, the conclusions are descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal proof of improved learning or reliable assessment accuracy.

title: Who Thinks First? Designing Productive Friction with Engage-to-Unlock GenAI
summary: Generative AI can support writing, but frictionless access may cause cognitive offloading before users develop their own ideas. We introduce Engage-to-Unlock, a productive-friction mechanism that unlocks generative capabilities after users meaningfully engage with the task. In a controlled experiment (N = 398), participants completed a writing task under one of four conditions: Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, Engage-to-Unlock, or Time-Matched Unlock, which matched unlock timing to Engage-to-Unlock participants but independent of users' engagement, then evaluated passages for evidence and inferential errors. Results show that Engage-to-Unlock redistributed effort across tasks: participants spent more time writing and less time evaluating, without increasing overall task duration. They also submitted more prompts than in other AI-assisted conditions and showed the highest accuracy-per-time evaluation efficiency across conditions. These findings suggest that designing GenAI access to encourage early human engagement may provide a productive form of friction, while retaining active AI use and efficient downstream evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether requiring users to engage with a writing task before unlocking generative AI improves human–AI collaboration. In a controlled experiment with 398 participants, Engage-to-Unlock increased early writing effort, reduced evaluation time, maintained total task duration, encouraged more prompting, and produced the highest evaluation accuracy per unit time among conditions.
AI.motivation: Frictionless access to generative AI may encourage cognitive offloading before users form their own ideas, potentially weakening independent engagement and later evaluation of AI-generated content. The paper is motivated by the need to design AI interfaces that preserve meaningful human effort without eliminating the productivity benefits of generative assistance.
AI.method: The authors conducted a controlled experiment with N = 398 participants performing a writing task under four conditions: Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, Engage-to-Unlock, and Time-Matched Unlock. In the Engage-to-Unlock condition, generative capabilities became available only after participants demonstrated meaningful engagement with the task. The Time-Matched Unlock condition provided access at a comparable time, but independently of engagement, allowing the study to distinguish the effect of engagement-based unlocking from a mere delay. Participants also evaluated passages for evidential and inferential errors, and the study measured time allocation, prompting behavior, task duration, and evaluation efficiency.
AI.result: Engage-to-Unlock shifted effort toward initial writing and away from downstream evaluation, without increasing overall task time. Participants in this condition submitted more prompts than those in other AI-assisted conditions and achieved the highest accuracy-per-time evaluation efficiency across all conditions. The findings indicate that engagement-based friction can preserve active AI use while improving the efficiency of evaluating generated content.
AI.conclusion: Engage-to-Unlock offers a productive-friction design for generative AI systems. Requiring early human engagement before granting AI assistance may reduce premature cognitive offloading, encourage users to develop initial ideas, and support efficient human oversight without imposing a greater total time cost. The results support designing AI access around users’ task engagement rather than relying solely on fixed delays.

title: Where LLMs Fail with Visualization DSLs
summary: As LLMs take up the role of authoring charts using visualization domain-specific languages (DSLs), the human constraints that shaped those languages may no longer apply, as what is easy for a person is not necessarily easy for a model. To understand how LLMs might work better with DSLs, we explore where and how they fail with current DSL designs. We evaluate 10 JSON-style visualization DSLs with 41 tasks across 3 LLMs, then assess the generated specifications with JSON and rendering checks, and qualitative coding of failed cases. Analyzing how this specification generation process fails, we identify four recurring failure patterns, link each to specific DSL features, and discuss design considerations for future DSL designs.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language models generate visualization specifications in JSON-style domain-specific languages (DSLs). It evaluates 10 DSLs on 41 tasks using 3 LLMs, checks both JSON validity and rendering success, and qualitatively analyzes failures. The study identifies four recurring failure patterns associated with particular DSL features and derives implications for designing visualization DSLs that better support LLM-based authoring.
AI.motivation: Visualization DSLs were historically designed around human authoring constraints, but LLMs have different strengths and weaknesses. As LLMs increasingly generate chart specifications, existing DSL designs may cause systematic errors even when they are usable by humans. The paper therefore investigates where LLMs fail with current JSON-style visualization DSLs and how DSL design could be adapted to better support model-based specification generation.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical evaluation of 10 JSON-style visualization DSLs across 41 visualization tasks and 3 LLMs. Generated specifications are assessed using structural JSON checks and rendering checks to determine whether outputs are syntactically valid and produce usable visualizations. The failed cases are then qualitatively coded to identify recurring failure patterns and connect them to specific DSL features.
AI.result: The analysis reveals four recurring patterns of LLM failure during visualization specification generation. These failures are linked to characteristics of existing DSLs, indicating that some design features impose difficulties on LLMs even when they may be reasonable for human users. The combined validity and rendering evaluation provides evidence that DSL choice and feature design materially affect LLM-generated visualization quality.
AI.conclusion: Visualization DSLs should not be designed solely around human authoring assumptions when LLMs are important authors. Future DSLs should account for model-specific failure modes, simplify or reorganize problematic features, and provide structures that improve reliable specification generation. The paper offers design considerations for developing LLM-oriented visualization DSLs.

title: XAI Evaluation Cards: A Practical Method for Designing Human-Centred XAI Evaluations
summary: Evaluating explainable AI (XAI) systems from a human-centred approach requires researchers to select from numerous evaluation dimensions and measures, often in an ad hoc and fragmented manner. This paper introduces a method to help HCI, computer science, designers and social science researchers systematically evaluate XAI systems. The approach is based on an updated XAI-specific evaluation framework derived from an analysis of 82 studies. Using this framework, we developed a card-sorting method with 36 cards to help researchers prioritise relevant evaluation aspects. The process was tested with two research groups (n = 13) across five projects. The XAI Evaluation Cards are available as a printable appendix, along with an online repository of methods from previous XAI studies. Although not exhaustive, our findings indicate that the card-sorting approach can organise and streamline the design of the evaluation process, encouraging a more comprehensive and multidisciplinary assessment of XAI systems in research and development.

AI.tldr: The paper presents XAI Evaluation Cards, a structured card-sorting method grounded in an updated framework from 82 prior studies, to help researchers systematically plan human-centred evaluations of explainable AI systems. Testing with 13 researchers across five projects suggests the method makes evaluation planning more organised, comprehensive, and multidisciplinary, though it is not exhaustive.
AI.motivation: Human-centred XAI evaluation involves many possible dimensions and measures, but researchers often select them inconsistently and ad hoc. The paper addresses the need for a systematic, practical method that supports researchers from HCI, computer science, design, and social science in identifying and prioritising suitable evaluation aspects.
AI.method: The authors analysed 82 XAI evaluation studies to update an XAI-specific evaluation framework. They then operationalised the framework as a card-sorting activity consisting of 36 evaluation cards. The approach was tested by two research groups involving 13 participants and spanning five projects. Supporting materials include printable cards and an online repository of methods used in earlier XAI research.
AI.result: The evaluation indicates that the card-sorting approach helps research teams organise and streamline the design of XAI evaluation processes. It supports prioritisation of relevant evaluation dimensions and encourages consideration of a broader range of methods and perspectives. The evidence is based on a small, practice-oriented test rather than a broad comparative validation.
AI.conclusion: XAI Evaluation Cards offer a useful structured aid for planning more comprehensive and multidisciplinary human-centred evaluations of XAI systems. The method can reduce fragmentation in evaluation design, but its framework and evidence should be treated as supportive rather than exhaustive or definitive.
